readings.title: A Prayer (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Untangle a few tightly packed sentences and follow a small story that turns into a joke at the speaker’s expense.
readings.focus: A speaker who took a promise word for word is smiled at by heaven, and draws a sly, rueful lesson about trust.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “A Prayer.” Jehovah is a name for God in the Hebrew Bible; cherubim are angels. To stipulate is to name a condition; “upon this wise” means in this way; extant means still existing. The promise quoted in the sixth stanza echoes Gospel sayings such as “Ask, and it shall be given you.”

excerpt.locator: Book I, “Life,” XIII, “A Prayer,” complete poem; opens “I MEANT to have but modest needs, Such as content, and heaven; Within my income these…”; closes “…With a suspicious air,— As children, swindled for the first, All swindlers be, infer.”.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker first mean to ask for, and why did she think it was a modest request?
facilitatorNotes: Contentment and heaven, which she thought lay “within my income,” so that she and life would “keep even,” like a careful household budget. Since heaven would include contentment, she decides to ask for heaven alone. Her money words make prayer sound like a sensible bargain.
evidence: Within my income these could lie,

questions.prompt: How do Jehovah, the cherubim and the saints react to her prayer? What do their reactions suggest?
facilitatorNotes: God smiles, the cherubim withdraw, and grave saints creep out to look at her and show “their dimples”: they are trying not to laugh. Readers may decide the amusement is fond, like grown-ups touched by a child’s earnest request, or mocking, which is how the speaker seems to take it.

questions.prompt: Reread the fifth and sixth stanzas. What does heaven find so funny?
facilitatorNotes: That anyone could still be honest enough to “take the tale for true,” believing that whatever you ask will be given. Even Judgment “twinkled.” Her mistake was taking a promise literally. Some readers think the joke is on her; others think it is on a promise that was never meant to be read that way.
evidence: As take the tale for true

questions.prompt: In the last stanza she has “grown shrewder.” Is the lesson she draws a fair one?
facilitatorNotes: She now watches the sky “with a suspicious air,” the way a child cheated once decides everyone is a cheat. Her own comparison admits the suspicion may be an overreaction: one swindle does not prove that all are swindlers. Readers can argue whether the poem laughs at the speaker, at the promise, or at both, and whether it is funny, sad or both.
evidence: But I, grown shrewder, scan the skies
As children, swindled for the first,

readings.title: Returning (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a short story told almost entirely through small movements of the hands, and infer the fear behind them.
readings.focus: A homecoming becomes too frightening to finish: the speaker fears finding that the life left behind is gone.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “Returning.” The speaker comes back after many years away and stops at the door of the old home. Nerve here means courage; a latch is the catch that holds a door shut.

excerpt.locator: Book I, “Life,” LIII, “Returning,” complete poem; opens “I YEARS had been from home, And now, before the door, I dared not open, lest a face I…”; closes “…As cautiously as glass, And held my ears, and like a thief Fled gasping from the house.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker fear will happen if the door is opened?
facilitatorNotes: That a stranger’s face will “stare vacant” and ask what business she has there. Her answer, “just a life I left,” shows the deeper fear: not the stranger but finding that her old life no longer lives in the house.
evidence: I dared not open, lest a face
My business,—just a life I left,

questions.prompt: List what the speaker does, from reaching the door to leaving. Which words show the fear growing?
facilitatorNotes: She fumbles at her nerve, scans the windows, listens to the silence, laughs a forced laugh, fits her hand to the latch “with trembling care,” lifts her fingers off as if from glass, holds her ears and flees “gasping.” The actions move from hesitation to panic, and she never opens the door.

questions.prompt: Why is the silence like an ocean that “broke against my ear”?
facilitatorNotes: Silence is the absence of sound, but here it rolls and crashes like waves: nothing has become overwhelming. Fear makes her hear the empty house as loud. Readers may say whether they have ever heard silence like that.
evidence: The silence like an ocean rolled,

questions.prompt: The speaker has faced “danger and the dead” but runs from a door. Why might a door be more frightening? Is her laugh at herself fair?
facilitatorNotes: Danger can be fought; a changed home cannot be fought or undone, and while the door stays shut, the old life may still be inside. The “wooden laugh” is stiff: she knows the fear looks foolish but cannot laugh it away, and she leaves “like a thief” from her own home. Some readers find the ending sad, others understandable, even wise, a way of keeping the old home whole in memory.
evidence: Who danger and the dead had faced,
And held my ears, and like a thief

readings.title: Hunger (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Read a poem that may be about real food or about anything long wanted, and test both readings against its words.
readings.focus: Getting what you have wanted for years can feel strange, and wanting may itself be a way of life that having ends.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “Hunger.” In Dickinson’s New England, dinner was the midday meal, so “My noon had come, to dine” means her time to eat had come at last. “Curious” here means rare or strange; ample means plentiful.

excerpt.locator: Book I, “Life,” L, “Hunger,” complete poem; opens “I HAD been hungry all the years; My noon had come, to dine; I, trembling, drew the table…”; closes “…so I found That hunger was a way Of persons outside windows, The entering takes away.”.

questions.prompt: Where had the speaker seen such food before, and where was she standing then?
facilitatorNotes: On other people’s tables, through windows, when she was “hungry, lone” and looking at wealth she “could not hope to own.” She was outside looking in.
evidence: I looked in windows, for the wealth
I could not hope to own.

questions.prompt: What did she share with the birds, and why does the “ample bread” seem unfamiliar?
facilitatorNotes: Crumbs, eaten outdoors “In Nature's dining-room.” She is used to very little, shared; a whole loaf is “so unlike the crumb” that she hardly recognizes it as food for her.

questions.prompt: Why does plenty hurt her? Explain the comparison with a berry bush.
facilitatorNotes: She feels “ill and odd,” like a wild mountain plant dug up and set by a road: moved out of the place it grew to fit. Something good can still be the wrong place for you. Readers might compare a first day somewhere grand or new.
evidence: The plenty hurt me, 't was so new,—

questions.prompt: What does she decide about hunger in the last stanza? Do you think the poem is only about food?
facilitatorNotes: She was no longer hungry; hunger, she finds, belongs to “persons outside windows,” and going in takes it away. Wanting had been part of who she was. Many readers take the poem to be about any long-wanted thing, such as success, love or belonging; others keep to the literal meal. Ask which words work both ways.

readings.title: The way I read a letter's this (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a step-by-step routine and work out what all that care shows about the reader’s feelings.
readings.focus: A comic ritual of privacy guards a letter whose writer the speaker will not reveal, even to us.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The poem stands in the book’s second part, “Love,” though it never names the letter’s writer. To counteract is to work against; “exorcised” means driven out, as an evil spirit is; to peruse is to read carefully; creeds are the official beliefs of churches. In Dickinson’s day letters were the only way to hear from someone far away.

excerpt.locator: Book II, “Love,” VI, complete poem; opens “THE way I read a letter's this: 'T is first I lock the door, And push it with my fingers…”; closes “…one that you know! And sigh for lack of heaven,—but not The heaven the creeds bestow.”.

questions.prompt: List each step the speaker takes before she reads.
facilitatorNotes: She locks the door, pushes it to be sure, goes as far off as she can in case someone knocks, draws the letter out, “picks its lock” (breaks the seal), then glances at wall and floor for a mouse. A long, careful routine for one small letter.
evidence: 'T is first I lock the door,

questions.prompt: Why check for a mouse? Is the speaker serious or making fun of herself?
facilitatorNotes: A mouse cannot read. Solemn words such as “firm conviction” and “exorcised,” used for a mouse, make the precaution comic. She knows she is being absurd, yet the joke shows how private the letter is: not even a mouse may share it.
evidence: For firm conviction of a mouse

questions.prompt: Who wrote the letter? What does the dash in “To—no one that you know!” do?
facilitatorNotes: She begins to tell us whom she is “infinite” to, then stops and shuts us out, as she shut the door. The poem keeps the very secret it describes. Readers may guess at a dear friend or someone loved; the poem gives no name.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the heaven she sighs for and “the heaven the creeds bestow”?
facilitatorNotes: The heaven of the churches comes after death; hers seems to be the happiness of being with the letter’s writer, here on earth. She sighs for “lack” of it, so the writer is probably far away. Some readers find it daring to set a person beside heaven; others hear simply how much the letter means to her.
evidence: And sigh for lack of heaven,—but not

readings.title: At Home (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow the poem from a wide, cold outdoors to one small room, and decide who is on the sofa.
readings.focus: A stormy November night makes home feel safe, and the last line shows that what makes it home is a person.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “At Home” and placed it in the book’s second part, “Love.” The eaves are the edges of a roof; blinds here are window shutters; plush is a thick soft cloth; sleet is half-frozen rain. “Thee” is an old word for “you,” used for someone dear.

excerpt.locator: Book II, “Love,” VIII, “At Home,” complete poem; opens “THE night was wide, and furnished scant With but a single star, That often as a cloud it…”; closes “…task. "How pleasanter," said she Unto the sofa opposite, "The sleet than May—no thee!"”.

questions.prompt: Find three details of the night outside. What kind of night is it?
facilitatorNotes: A single star that “blew out itself for fear” whenever a cloud passed; wind chasing the bush and fretting in the eaves; no squirrel out; one late dog. It is cold, windy and almost empty: a night to stay in.

questions.prompt: How can a dog’s feet sound “like intermittent plush”? What does the comparison let you hear?
facilitatorNotes: Intermittent means stopping and starting; plush is soft thick cloth. The paws pad softly, now and then, down the empty street, a soft sound in a hard night. The poem listens as closely as it looks.

questions.prompt: What does the housewife do indoors, and why does she “shiver for the poor”?
facilitatorNotes: She checks the shutters and draws her rocking-chair closer to the fire. Her own comfort makes her think of people without shelter on such a night; the shiver is sympathy, not cold.

questions.prompt: Reread the last two lines. Who is on “the sofa opposite,” and what does she mean?
facilitatorNotes: Most readers think someone she loves sits across from her: she would rather have sleet with him than May without him (“no thee”). A few read the sofa as empty and the words as missing someone. Either way, the poem ends by showing that the warmth of home is a person, not the fire.

readings.title: In the Garden (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a poem that moves from plain watching to a dazzling comparison, and find the line where it changes.
readings.focus: A bird is first a small, nervous creature eating and drinking, then, in flight, something smoother than oars or swimming butterflies.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “In the Garden.” An angle-worm is an earthworm, the kind anglers use as bait. A seam here is the line a boat cuts in water; plashless means without a splash.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XXIII, “In the Garden,” complete poem; opens “A BIRD came down the walk: He did not know I saw; He bit an angle-worm in halves And ate…”; closes “…Too silver for a seam, Or butterflies, off banks of noon, Leap, plashless, as they swim.”.

questions.prompt: What does the bird do before it knows it is watched? Which detail surprises you?
facilitatorNotes: It bites a worm in half and eats it raw, drinks dew from a blade of grass, and hops sideways to let a beetle pass. The worm is blunt and comic (“the fellow”); stepping aside for a beetle is almost polite.
evidence: He bit an angle-worm in halves

questions.prompt: How do the bird’s eyes show what it feels? Why “frightened beads”?
facilitatorNotes: They glance quickly everywhere, small, round and shiny like beads, and frightened. “I thought” shows the speaker knows this is her own reading of the bird.
evidence: They looked like frightened beads, I thought;

questions.prompt: What happens when the speaker offers a crumb? Who is “cautious”?
facilitatorNotes: The bird flies off rather than take it. Because “cautious” ends a line, it can belong to the bird, “Like one in danger,” or to the speaker offering the crumb. Both are careful of each other; ask readers which they choose.

questions.prompt: The bird “rowed him softer home.” Explain the comparisons in the last stanza and why the poem ends with them.
facilitatorNotes: Wings are like oars, but softer than oars dividing the ocean, leaving no seam; or like butterflies leaping off “banks of noon” without a splash. Air becomes water and flying becomes rowing and swimming. The plain garden scene ends in wonder; readers may say whether the ending is more about the bird or about the speaker’s delight.

readings.title: Old-Fashioned (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Tell when the speaker is joking and when she is worried, in a poem that does both at once.
readings.focus: A speaker who loves things by their plain names objects, half in fun, to science that measures, classes and maps them, and wonders whether heaven itself will change.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “Old-Fashioned.” Arcturus is one of the brightest stars. Stamens are the pollen-bearing parts of a flower; scientists of Dickinson’s day sorted plants into classes partly by counting them, and collectors pinned butterflies in cabinets. The zenith is the point of the sky straight overhead; a stile is a set of steps over a fence.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XX, “Old-Fashioned,” complete poem; opens “ARCTURUS is his other name,— I'd rather call him star! It's so unkind of science To go…”; closes “…Will lift his little girl,— Old-fashioned, naughty, everything,— Over the stile of pearl!”.

questions.prompt: What has science done to the star, the flower and the butterfly?
facilitatorNotes: Given the star another name, Arcturus; counted the flower’s stamens and put her “in a class”; pinned the butterfly in a cabinet. Each time, something the speaker knew as a friend becomes a specimen.
evidence: Computes the stamens in a breath,

questions.prompt: Why call the scientist “A monster with a glass”? Is she serious?
facilitatorNotes: The glass is a magnifying lens; “monster” is a child’s exaggeration for a grown-up who spoils a game, and “so unkind of science” sounds like a playful complaint. Readers can disagree about how much she means it: science is not shown doing harm, only changing how things are seen.

questions.prompt: What worries her about heaven in the fourth to sixth stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: Heaven has become “zenith,” a point to be mapped and charted. She wonders whether the kingdom of Heaven has changed and whether its children will be “new-fashioned” and laugh at her. Behind the joke is a real fear that what she was taught to hope for may not survive the new knowledge.
evidence: Won't be new-fashioned when I come,

questions.prompt: How does she picture herself at the end, and how does that connect with the title?
facilitatorNotes: As a little girl, “Old-fashioned, naughty, everything,” hoping to be lifted over heaven’s gate as over a country fence. She claims being old-fashioned with pride. Ask whether readers side with her or with the scientist, or think one person could love both naming and counting.

readings.title: Going to heaven! (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a speaker who changes her mind, perhaps more than once, and decide what she finally believes.
readings.focus: Talk of heaven is first wonder and gentle teasing, until the last stanza admits doubt and shows why other people’s belief still matters to her.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The book’s fourth part, “Time and Eternity,” gathers poems about death and what may follow it. The poem opens by repeating something just said, “Going to heaven!” Hymns and sermons of Dickinson’s day promised the faithful a white robe and a crown in heaven.
readings.contentNote: The speaker thinks of two people she has lost and of the afternoon she “left them in the ground.”

excerpt.locator: Book IV, “Time and Eternity,” II, complete poem; opens “GOING to heaven! I don't know when, Pray do not ask me how,— Indeed, I'm too astonished…”; closes “…it Whom I have never found Since the mighty autumn afternoon I left them in the ground.”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker react to the words “Going to heaven!” in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: She is “too astonished” to say when or how; the idea sounds “dim,” far off and unclear. Yet she says it will happen “As sure as flocks go home at night.” Wonder and certainty sit side by side.
evidence: As sure as flocks go home at night

questions.prompt: What does she ask the listener to do if they arrive first? Why are “robe” and “crown” in quotation marks?
facilitatorNotes: Save her a little place near “the two I lost.” The quotation marks treat robe and crown as other people’s words, the language of hymns and sermons, as though she were half quoting rather than fully believing. She wants only the smallest robe and a bit of crown: the people matter more than the finery.
evidence: Close to the two I lost!

questions.prompt: “I'm glad I don't believe it.” What reason does she give, and does it surprise you after the first three stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: Believing would “stop my breath,” and she wants to look longer at “such a curious earth.” This reverses the eager tone of the opening. Some readers think the earlier stanzas were playful all along; others think she truly swings between belief and doubt.
evidence: I'm glad I don't believe it,

questions.prompt: Why is she glad that the people she lost did believe it? What do the last lines show about her?
facilitatorNotes: Their faith comforted them; she has not “found” them since the autumn afternoon of their burial. She can doubt for herself and still be glad for them. The plain words “I left them in the ground” show grief beneath the playful tone. Readers may judge whether the poem ends in doubt, in hope, or in both.
evidence: I am glad they did believe it
I left them in the ground.

readings.title: Memorials (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Untangle the first stanza’s word order, then follow two examples to the feeling they share.
readings.focus: After a death, small unfinished things become precious, and grief changes even the act of reading.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “Memorials.” The first stanza means: death makes us notice things our eyes had hurried past, as if (“except” here means “unless”) a person who has died were gently begging us to look. A perished creature is a person who has died; crayon here means drawing and wool means knitting; a thimble protects the finger in sewing.
readings.contentNote: A poem of grief: things left behind by people who have died.

excerpt.locator: Book IV, “Time and Eternity,” XIII, “Memorials,” complete poem; opens “Death sets a thing significant The eye had hurried by, Except a perished creature Entreat…”; closes “…read, I read not, For interrupting tears Obliterate the etchings Too costly for repairs.”.

questions.prompt: What is the first “little workmanship”? What does “This was last her fingers did” tell you?
facilitatorNotes: A drawing or a piece of knitting or needlework, left unfinished; someone says it was the last thing her fingers made. An ordinary object becomes important because it was the last.
evidence: With "This was last her fingers did,"

questions.prompt: How does the poem show her growing weaker, without saying she was ill?
facilitatorNotes: The thimble “weighed too heavy,” the “stitches stopped themselves,” and the work was put away on a closet shelf. Death is shown by small things stopping. The stitches seem to stop on their own, as if no one were to blame.

questions.prompt: What is the second example, and how is it different from the first?
facilitatorNotes: A book from a friend, with his pencil marks beside the places he liked. The first is something the dead woman made; the second is a trace of what the friend thought and enjoyed. In both, the hands are now still: “At rest his fingers are.”
evidence: Had notched the place that pleased him,—

questions.prompt: “Now, when I read, I read not.” What does she mean, and why are the marks “Too costly for repairs”?
facilitatorNotes: Tears blur the page, so she cannot read the book; she is reading her friend, not the words. The pencil marks are “etchings” no one can redo, because the person who made them is gone. Some readers find the ending hopeless; others feel the tears show how much the friend still matters.
evidence: Now, when I read, I read not,

readings.title: The Robin (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a poem built on one repeated line, and notice what changes from stanza to stanza.
readings.focus: The robin is first a noisy messenger of spring, then a flood of song, and last a silent teacher on her nest.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Robin.” The American robin, a large thrush with an orange-red breast, is one of the first birds to come back and sing in a New England spring, often before dawn. Express reports are urgent messages; cherubic means like a cherub, a plump little angel; certainty is being sure; sanctity is holiness.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” VI, “The Robin,” complete poem; opens “THE robin is the one That interrupts the morn With hurried, few, express reports When…”; closes “…one That speechless from her nest Submits that home and certainty And sanctity are best.”.

questions.prompt: Each stanza begins “The robin is the one.” What is the robin “the one” to do each time?
facilitatorNotes: To interrupt the morning in early March, to overflow the noon in April, and to show from her nest that home is best. The poem moves from morning to noon and from March to April, and from song to silence.

questions.prompt: What do the robin’s first songs sound like? Why might the poem call them “reports”?
facilitatorNotes: Short and urgent: “hurried, few, express,” like news brought by a messenger who cannot stop. The news is that spring is coming, though March has barely begun. “Interrupts” suggests the songs break into a quiet, sleepy morning; some readers will hear a little annoyance at being woken, others only delight.

questions.prompt: How can a bird “overflow the noon”? What might “cherubic quantity” mean?
facilitatorNotes: By April there is so much robin song that it spills over the whole middle of the day, like water over the brim of a cup. “Cherubic quantity” could be the amount of song, or the round, plump robin herself, like a chubby angel; the phrase holds both.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the robin says nothing. How does she teach that home is best without speaking?
facilitatorNotes: By sitting quietly on her nest: her example says what her songs never did. The noisy first stanzas make her silence stand out. Some readers think the lesson is the speaker’s own feeling read into the bird; Dickinson herself rarely left her family home.

readings.title: The Butterfly’s Day (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a comparison that runs through a whole poem, and decide what the poem thinks of an idle day.
readings.focus: A butterfly goes out like a fine lady for an aimless summer afternoon, while bees and haymakers work, until sunset puts out them all.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Butterfly’s Day.” A cocoon is the case in which a caterpillar changes; “repairing” means going; miscellaneous enterprise is business of every sort; a parasol is a lady’s sunshade, here the butterfly’s wings; contracting means closing up; phantom means ghostly; circumference here means circling; a tropic show is a brilliant display from hot countries; zealous means eager; to disdain is to look down on; extinguished means put out, like a light.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” VII, “The Butterfly’s Day,” complete poem; opens “FROM cocoon forth a butterfly As lady from her door Emerged—a summer afternoon— Repairing…”; closes “…tide, And men that made the hay, And afternoon, and butterfly, Extinguished in its sea.”.

questions.prompt: The butterfly comes out “As lady from her door.” Find other words that keep up the picture of a lady.
facilitatorNotes: She goes “Repairing everywhere” as a lady goes visiting; her wings are a “pretty parasol”; she meets “parties” like guests at a garden party; she and her friends are an “audience” looking down on the workers. The whole poem dresses the butterfly as a lady of leisure.

questions.prompt: Where does the butterfly go, and what is she trying to do?
facilitatorNotes: Nowhere in particular: “Without design, that I could trace.” She visits the clover, closes her wings over a hayfield, struggles against a cloud, and joins other butterflies circling “To Nowhere.” Her business is understood only by the clovers.
evidence: Without design, that I could trace,

questions.prompt: Who is working in this poem, and who is idle? Does the poem admire the butterfly or make fun of her?
facilitatorNotes: The bee, the flower and the haymakers work; the butterflies are an “audience of idleness” that disdains them. The tone is playful: the poem enjoys her beauty and her aimlessness but smiles at her airs. Readers can argue either way from “purposeless circumference” and “tropic show.”

questions.prompt: What happens at sundown? Why are the haymakers put out along with the butterfly?
facilitatorNotes: Evening comes like a tide and puts out the men, the afternoon and the butterfly together, as the sea puts out a flame. Workers and idlers end the day the same way. Some readers hear only the close of a summer day; others hear a hint of death, because “extinguished” is so final.
evidence: Till sundown crept, a steady tide,

readings.title: The Bluebird (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Picture the bird from a few surprising words, and decide whom his song is for.
readings.focus: A weather-worn bluebird arrives before anyone expects spring and sings for the joy of it on a bare tree.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Bluebird.” The eastern bluebird is one of the first birds back in a New England spring, often while the trees are still bare; the male is bright blue above with a rusty-brown breast. A surmise is a guess; inspiriting means cheering; habiliments are clothes; indigo is deep blue; specimens are samples; discretion is good judgement; seraphic means like a seraph, a shining angel.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” VIII, “The Bluebird,” complete poem; opens “BEFORE you thought of spring, Except as a surmise, You see, God bless his suddenness, A…”; closes “…superior tree Without a single leaf, And shouts for joy to nobody But his seraphic self!”.

questions.prompt: When does the bluebird come, and how does the speaker feel about it?
facilitatorNotes: Before you have really thought of spring, when it is only a guess. He appears suddenly, and she is delighted: “God bless his suddenness.”
evidence: You see, God bless his suddenness,

questions.prompt: Describe the bird’s clothes. Why might he be “A little weather-worn”?
facilitatorNotes: He wears “habiliments / Of indigo and brown,” blue and rusty brown, bright enough to cheer anyone. He is a little worn because he has flown a long way north and arrived while the weather is still rough, like a traveller in a dusty coat.

questions.prompt: “With specimens of song, / As if for you to choose.” What is the bird doing, and why might it sound like choosing?
facilitatorNotes: He sings short phrases with pauses between them, “gay delays,” as a shopkeeper might lay out samples for a customer to pick from. The bluebird’s song really is a few soft, separate notes.

questions.prompt: He “shouts for joy to nobody / But his seraphic self!” Was the song for us after all?
facilitatorNotes: The first stanza imagined the song offered for us to choose; the end admits he sings for himself, on a tree without a leaf, with no audience needed. Some readers find that joyful, joy for its own sake; others feel a little shut out, or think the speaker is laughing at herself for thinking it was meant for her.
evidence: As if for you to choose,
And shouts for joy to nobody

readings.title: The Humming-Bird (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Read a poem that never names its subject, and work out how it shows something too fast to see.
readings.focus: In eight lines a hummingbird flashes past, ruffles the flowers and is gone, perhaps all the way to Africa.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The poem has no title of its own; the 1891 editors called it “The Humming-Bird.” The ruby-throated hummingbird is the only hummingbird common in the eastern United States: its wings beat so fast they blur and hum, its back shines green, and the male’s throat is red. Evanescence means vanishing quickly; resonance is a ringing or humming sound; cochineal is a deep red dye; Tunis is a city in North Africa, far across the ocean.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XV, “The Humming-Bird,” complete poem; opens “A ROUTE of evanescence With a revolving wheel; A resonance of emerald, A rush of…”; closes “…bush Adjusts its tumbled head,— The mail from Tunis, probably, An easy morning's ride.”.

questions.prompt: Imagine reading the poem without its title. Which details would let you guess the bird?
facilitatorNotes: The “revolving wheel” of blurred wings, the hum (“resonance”), the green (“emerald”) and red (“cochineal”), the flowers left shaking, and the speed. The poem names colours and sounds, not a bird, because that is all the eye catches.

questions.prompt: What is “A route of evanescence”? Why might the poem begin there?
facilitatorNotes: A path of vanishing: you see only the line where something has been, not the thing itself. By the time you notice a hummingbird it is already gone, so the poem starts with its track.

questions.prompt: What do the flowers do after the bird has gone? What does “tumbled” tell you?
facilitatorNotes: Each blossom “Adjusts its tumbled head,” like someone smoothing their hair after a gust of wind. The bird was there long enough to knock them about, and the flowers prove it.
evidence: And every blossom on the bush

questions.prompt: “The mail from Tunis, probably, / An easy morning’s ride.” Is the speaker serious?
facilitatorNotes: It is a deadpan joke: the bird is so fast it might be a mail rider who left Africa this morning and finds the trip easy. “Probably” makes it funnier. There is a grain of truth, since hummingbirds really do migrate thousands of miles. Some readers take the bird to be bringing news, like a letter; that reading fits too.

readings.title: The Rat (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a joke that treats an animal as a lodger, and notice how the poem’s shape fits its subject.
readings.focus: The rat lives in our house rent-free, outwits us, and has as much right to be there as nature itself.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Rat.” A tenant rents a home from a landlord. Concise means short and to the point; to repudiate is to refuse to accept; an obligation is a duty, here paying rent; to balk is to block; to sound is to find something out, and to circumvent is to get round it; reticent means silent and secretive; a decree is an official order; equilibrium is balance, here the balance of nature.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XXXV, “The Rat,” complete poem; opens “The rat is the concisest tenant. He pays no rent,— Repudiates the obligation, On schemes…”; closes “Neither decree Prohibits him, Lawful as Equilibrium.”.

questions.prompt: The rat is called a “tenant.” What kind of tenant is he?
facilitatorNotes: The worst kind for a landlord: he “pays no rent” and refuses even to admit he owes it, busy with his own plans. “Concisest” makes him the smallest, quietest, most tucked-away lodger in the house.
evidence: The rat is the concisest tenant.

questions.prompt: What do people try to do about the rat, and how does it go?
facilitatorNotes: They try to find him out and get round him, but he blocks their cleverness (“Balking our wit”). They can hate him, but hate cannot reach a creature that never shows himself or says a word.

questions.prompt: Look at the lengths of the lines as the poem goes on. How does the shape suit a rat?
facilitatorNotes: The lines grow shorter and shorter until the last stanza is almost nothing, “Lawful as / Equilibrium.” The poem itself is concise, slipping away like the rat into a small hole.

questions.prompt: The rat is “Lawful as / Equilibrium.” What is the poem saying about his right to be there? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: No human order forbids him; he belongs to the balance of nature, which needs no one’s permission. The poem half admires him. Readers who have dealt with rats, or know they can spread disease, may disagree; others may enjoy the joke that the landlord has no say.

readings.title: A Thunder-Storm (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a storm step by step, and notice how almost everything in it behaves like a living creature.
readings.focus: Wind, leaves, dust, thunder and lightning act out a summer storm until the rain breaks like a flood and just misses the speaker’s home.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “A Thunder-Storm.” A menace is a threat; livid means bluish-grey, or furious; dams hold back water; to quarter is to split into pieces, as lightning can split a tree.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XXXVII, “A Thunder-Storm,” complete poem; opens “THE wind begun to rock the grass With threatening tunes and low,— He flung a menace at…”; closes “…The waters wrecked the sky, But overlooked my father's house, Just quartering a tree.”.

questions.prompt: Put the storm in order. What happens first, what next, and what last?
facilitatorNotes: The wind rocks the grass and threatens; leaves fly and dust blows; wagons hurry, thunder rolls, lightning flashes; birds and cattle take shelter; one giant drop falls, then the downpour; the storm passes over the house and splits a tree.
evidence: THE wind begun to rock the grass
There came one drop of giant rain,

questions.prompt: “The dust did scoop itself like hands / And throw away the road.” What else in the poem acts like a living thing?
facilitatorNotes: The wind flings threats, the leaves unhook themselves, the lightning has a beak and a claw like a bird of prey, the birds “put up the bars” like people locking doors, and unseen hands hold the dams. Nature becomes a crowd of creatures acting out the storm.
evidence: The leaves unhooked themselves from trees
The lightning showed a yellow beak,

questions.prompt: How can thunder hurry slowly?
facilitatorNotes: Thunder rolls on in a long, slow rumble, yet the storm is coming on fast; the phrase holds both. Some readers hear the slow thunder against the hurrying wagons in the line before.
evidence: The wagons quickened on the streets,

questions.prompt: The storm “overlooked my father's house, / Just quartering a tree.” How does the speaker feel at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Relieved: the house was spared. But “Just” is an understatement, since a tree split in four is a frightening near miss. “Overlooked” can mean passed over and also looked down on. Readers may hear calm, or fear held in.

readings.title: November (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Find the season the poem describes, and notice how it talks back to other poets.
readings.focus: Dickinson writes about the plain grey days between autumn’s colour and the first snow, which other poets leave out.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “November.” Prosaic means plain and ordinary, the opposite of poetic; incisive means sharp, cutting; ascetic means bare and self-denying, like a hermit. William Cullen Bryant was a famous American poet who wrote about autumn and the goldenrod, a yellow wildflower; James Thomson, a Scottish poet, wrote about harvest sheaves, bundles of cut grain. Valves are things that open and shut; mesmeric means hypnotising.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XLIX, “November,” complete poem; opens “BESIDES the autumn poets sing, A few prosaic days A little this side of the snow And that…”; closes “…remain, My sentiments to share. Grant me, O Lord, a sunny mind, Thy windy will to bear!”.

questions.prompt: Exactly when in the year is this? Find the lines that place it.
facilitatorNotes: After the autumn that poets sing about and before the snow: “A little this side of the snow / And that side of the haze,” the soft haze of an autumn warm spell. That is November.
evidence: A little this side of the snow
And that side of the haze.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem mention Mr. Bryant’s goldenrod and Mr. Thomson’s sheaves?
facilitatorNotes: Other poets wrote about autumn’s beauty, the yellow flowers and the harvest; those are gone now. She chooses the “prosaic” days nobody writes about. Calling the poets “Mr.” is gently teasing, as if they were neighbours.

questions.prompt: What has gone still or closed in the third stanza? Who might the “elves” be?
facilitatorNotes: The busy brook is quiet, perhaps freezing; spicy things, perhaps seed pods or buds, are sealed shut; and soft fingers put “many elves” to sleep. The elves could be insects, small animals going into winter sleep, or flowers, or fairy-folk: the poem leaves it open.
evidence: Still is the bustle in the brook,

questions.prompt: The poem ends with a prayer. What does she ask for, and why might November need it?
facilitatorNotes: Only a squirrel may stay to share her feelings, so the days are lonely and bare. She asks God for a “sunny mind” to bear his “windy will”: both the cold winds and whatever else he sends. Some readers hear a joke in “windy”; others a serious wish for courage.

readings.title: The Blue Jay (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Follow a portrait that makes a bird both a soldier and a neighbour, and weigh the argument at the end.
readings.focus: The bold blue jay plays in the snow while the sky frowns, and the speaker protests that heaven should not leave him out.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Blue Jay.” The blue jay is a loud, crested blue bird that stays all through the New England winter. A brigadier is an army officer; civic means public-spirited; felicity is happiness; to censure is to scold; temerity is reckless boldness; pompous means self-important; nutriment is food; pungent means sharp-smelling; evergreens keep their needles all winter; a larder is a food store; terse means short and sharp; a tonic is a medicine that perks you up. Immortality is life after death; in Dickinson’s time people argued over whether animals had any.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” LI, “The Blue Jay,” complete poem; opens “NO brigadier throughout the year So civic as the jay. A neighbor and a warrior too, With…”; closes “…a tonic, His future a dispute; Unfair an immortality That leaves this neighbor out.”.

questions.prompt: The jay is “A neighbor and a warrior too.” Which words make him a soldier, and which a neighbour?
facilitatorNotes: Soldier: brigadier, warrior, “daring head,” a “militant” larder. Neighbour: “civic,” “neighbor,” “brother of the universe,” friendly with the snow. He is a bold soldier who is also good company.
evidence: A neighbor and a warrior too,

questions.prompt: What does the jay do on a harsh February day? How is he different from the people in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: He chases the scolding winds and is never blown away; he plays with the snow. The winds “censure us”: people shrink from the weather that the jay enjoys.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker feel an apology is due to the sky?
facilitatorNotes: The sky frowns pompously, but its frown only feeds the boldness of the jay and the snow, like a stern teacher whose frown makes cheeky children worse. The speaker jokingly feels sorry for the insulted sky.

questions.prompt: “Unfair an immortality / That leaves this neighbor out.” What is the speaker arguing? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: If heaven is only for people, it would be unfair, since a creature so full of life and character deserves a place too. Readers may agree, disagree, or think she says it half as a joke and half in earnest; the line “His future a dispute” shows that the question was argued in her day.

readings.title: The Oriole (1891 text)
readings.challenge: Collect the many names the poem gives one bird, and follow its jokes about gold and treasure.
readings.focus: The golden oriole is a thief, a cheat and a glorious singer, and the speaker finds in an apple tree the treasure heroes sailed the world to seek.
readings.context: This is the complete poem as printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd five years after Emily Dickinson’s death; she published almost nothing in her lifetime. Early editors changed her punctuation and sometimes her wording, and gave some poems titles; this reading keeps that historical published version. The 1891 editors titled it “The Oriole.” The Baltimore oriole is a brilliant orange-and-black songbird that comes north in May and feeds on fruit and nectar in orchards. In Greek myth King Midas turned everything he touched to gold, and Jason sailed with heroes to win the Golden Fleece. A prodigal spends wildly; to disavow is to deny; badinage is teasing talk; an alighting mine is a gold mine coming down to land; a dissembler is a pretender; an epicure loves fine food; betimes means at times; an oratorio is a great work of music for voices; attar is perfume made from flowers; decamping means leaving in a hurry; Burma (spelt “Burmah”) was famous for rubies and golden temples; bards are poets; an emolument is a payment or treasure.
readings.contentNote: The poem calls the bird “The Jesuit of orchards,” using an old prejudice that treated Jesuits, members of a Catholic religious order, as cunning deceivers.

excerpt.locator: Book III, “Nature,” XIII, “The Oriole,” complete poem; opens “ONE of the ones that Midas touched, Who failed to touch us all, Was that confiding…”; closes “…if there were a Jason, Tradition suffer me Behold his lost emolument Upon the apple-tree.”.

questions.prompt: “One of the ones that Midas touched” tells you the oriole’s colour. Find other gold and glitter in the poem.
facilitatorNotes: He is “So dazzling, we mistake him / For an alighting mine”; he has “The splendor of a Burmah”; he is “The meteor of birds”; and at the end he is the Golden Fleece itself, on the apple tree. Gold runs through the whole poem.
evidence: ONE of the ones that Midas touched,

questions.prompt: Stanza three gives the bird six names. Which are praise and which are blame? Why both?
facilitatorNotes: Dissembler, epicure and thief are blame, pleader nearly so; oratorio and “ecstasy in chief” are praise. He steals fruit and nectar and sings gloriously, so he “cheats as he enchants.” The poem cannot decide whether to scold or applaud him, and enjoys not deciding.

questions.prompt: “The Jesuit of orchards” uses a group of real people as a word for a sly cheat. What does the speaker mean, and is it fair to use people that way?
facilitatorNotes: She means a charming trickster who wins you over while he robs you. The word comes from an old Protestant prejudice against the Jesuits, a Catholic order. Readers should see that it is a stereotype: judging a whole group by a label is unfair, and we would not use the word this way now. Some may suggest a better word of their own.

questions.prompt: The speaker never believed Jason went after a golden fleece. If there were a Jason, where would his treasure be? What is the joke?
facilitatorNotes: On the apple tree: the oriole is the golden fleece, a treasure in a country orchard that no hero needed to sail for. The “rural man, / With thoughts that make for peace” finds wonders at home instead of in war and adventure. Some readers hear the humble speaker as teasing the old heroes; others as quietly boasting.
evidence: But then I am a rural man,
